title: Keep a scorebook: the game after the game
description: The notebook in the picture is where games go to be understood. A scorebook — moves, scores, dates, one honest line about what happened — turns matches you played into lessons you keep.

body.heading: One page per game
paragraphs: Give every game a page: the date, the players, the result, and the turning point in a single sentence. Chess players write the moves themselves; for any other game, the score by rounds and one line — 'lost the lead at the market card' — is enough.
The turning-point line is the treasure. Scores tell you who won; the turning point tells you why, and the why is the only part you can practise.

body.heading: Read it monthly
paragraphs: Once a month, read the scorebook through. Patterns step forward: you always fade in long games, you always win the rematch, one opponent's opening always troubles you. None of that is visible from inside a single game.
A scorebook also settles the oldest argument in games — who is really ahead between two rivals — with evidence instead of mythology. Keep it kindly: it is a record, not a weapon.

takeaway: One page per game — date, players, result, and the turning point in one sentence — read monthly, turns matches into lessons and rivalry into evidence.
